title: ADHD Detection from Short and Long Brain Patterns
one_liner: Watch both fast-changing and stable brain patterns to catch ADHD instead of looking at just one timescale.
lead: ADHD is a brain condition that shows up in how different regions activate and talk to each other. Most detection methods focus on what the brain does over long stretches of time, but they miss the quick, moment-to-moment shifts in activity. This paper captures both timescales because ADHD reveals itself in two ways: split-second reorganizations (bursts of mis-coordination) and long-term wiring weaknesses (stable structural problems). Fusing these catches what either alone would miss.

problem.h2: Brain patterns at one speed miss the full picture
paras: ADHD is a disorder where the brain's regions do not coordinate well — some fire when they should stay quiet, others stay quiet when they should fire. We diagnose it by scanning the brain and looking for these mis-coordinations.

A beginner might say: look at the brain image and see which regions are lit up. The problem: the brain does not hold still for one long look. It reorganizes its activity from second to second. Focusing only on the slow, stable patterns misses the fast reorganizations that are markers of ADHD. It is like trying to diagnose a heart condition by averaging the EKG tape over an hour — you lose the arrhythmias that happen in bursts.

callout.html: The method watches both rapid shifts and stable patterns in brain activity, then combines them for better diagnosis, because each timescale reveals different ADHD signatures that single-speed methods miss.

steps.b: Split the brain timeline into short chunks
steps.text: Slide a window across the brain images and extract activity at each microsecond-scale moment.
Encode how the brain's regions shift their coordination from chunk to chunk.
Use a graph neural network to extract the stable structural wiring (which regions are connected over the whole scan).
Store the history of short-term states to recognize recurring brain-state cycles.
Combine fast reorganization, long-term structure, and pattern memory into one diagnosis.

paras: Instead of extracting features at a single timescale, the method builds two parallel encoders: one that chases the fast, moment-to-moment shifts in brain coordination, and another that captures the slow, stable wiring structure. These flow together into a unified diagnosis.
object.object: the timescale and memory of brain pattern encoding

hidden.h2: Brain function memory: the recurring coordination patterns
hidden.name: brain function memory: recurring state cycles
paras: The paper introduces a named quantity called brain function memory. It is not a single brain region; it is a record of the repeating loops of coordination that the brain cycles through. When a person with ADHD concentrates, their brain's regions snap into a certain pattern; a few seconds later, they drift; then snap back. A healthy brain cycles through these states in a more stable, predictable rhythm. ADHD shows up as random jumbling of the cycle.

The method estimates this by training a memory graph network — a machine-learning model that sees a sequence of brain states and learns which states tend to follow each other. It then uses that learned memory to flag when the sequence is irregular (a sign of ADHD).

heat.caption: Darker means more strongly encoded in the memory. Strong repeats signal healthy rhythm; weak ones signal ADHD.

reads.html: The brain falls into a few favorite patterns of coordination, cycles through them, and then repeats. ADHD brains jump around instead of cycling smoothly.
The memory graph network learns the transition probabilities between brain states. When the real brain deviates from its learned rhythm, the network flags irregularity.

mechanism.h2: Why capturing both timescales fixes the detection
paras: The core reason this works: ADHD is visible at TWO different speeds. At the fast scale (fractions of a second), the brain's regions mis-coordinate in bursts — they activate and deactivate out of sync. At the slow scale (across the full scan), the wiring graph shows weaker connections between key hubs. A method that only looks at one scale catches a false negative. This method looks at both, so nothing hides.

Here is the causal chain: when you slice the brain timeline into short windows, you see the coordination breakdowns as they happen — a region lighting up when it should stay quiet. The encoder learns these fast reorganization patterns. Separately, a graph neural network follows the stable wiring. Then the memory network sees which fast patterns repeat, which is where ADHD reveals itself — the rhythm is jagged instead of smooth. By fusing all three (fast encoder + slow graph + memory), the diagnosis becomes much harder to fool.

stages.s: Extract slow structural wiring with graph neural network

math.h2: The core equation: fused feature scoring
math.words: diagnosis score equals weighted short-term memory plus weighted long-term graph features
math.equation: score = alpha * memory_score(short_states) + beta * graph_score(wiring) + gamma * encoder_state(current_window)
symbols: irregularity flag from the learned state-cycle memory
the sequence of fast brain-state snapshots
how disconnected the wiring is from a healthy brain
learned weights that balance the three signals

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a brain's fast patterns score 0.8 (quite irregular), and its graph score is 0.6 (somewhat disconnected). The memory flagged the state jumps as chaotic, adding 0.4. Using alpha=0.5, beta=0.3, gamma=0.2: final = 0.5 * 0.4 + 0.3 * 0.6 + 0.2 * 0.8 = 0.2 + 0.18 + 0.16 = 0.54.

A score of 0.54 (out of 1) signals ADHD. A healthy brain might score 0.15, where the memory cycle is smooth (0.1), the graph is well-connected (0.2), and fast patterns are orderly (0.3): 0.5 * 0.1 + 0.3 * 0.2 + 0.2 * 0.3 = 0.05 + 0.06 + 0.06 = 0.17. The gap between 0.54 and 0.17 is wide enough for a clear diagnosis.

math.note: All three components must align to signal ADHD; a single noisy view does not dominate.

items.html: If the short windows are not actually short, they average out the fast reorganizations, and you are back to the slow-only problem. The window must be short enough to see bursts of mis-coordination.

items.b: Memory network overfits to one person's quirks.
items.html: If the memory is trained on a small group, it learns that person's unique state cycles as if they were markers of ADHD, giving false positives on new subjects. It needs diverse training data.

items.b: Graph neural network misses weak or delayed connections.
items.html: Some ADHD brains have connections that are intact but slow (signals take longer to travel). A graph built from static snapshots may score them as normal wiring when they are not.
Use small windows, validate on independent data, and test sensitivity to connection delays.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small dataset: take 20 brain scans (10 ADHD, 10 control), slice them into windows, extract short-term reorganization patterns (lists of numbers describing how coordination changes), compute the graph of brain-region connections, and train a memory network on the sequences. Then withhold 4 new scans and measure diagnosis accuracy. The demo must show that dropping any one component (fast, slow, or memory) causes accuracy to fall; dropping all three and using only averages reduces it most. The gain from the fusion is visible.
demo.metric_eq: diagnosis_accuracy = correct_ADHD_calls / total_scans; also_report: recall (catch ADHD), precision (avoid false alarms), and drop_curve (accuracy when each component is removed)
demo.closing: The demo proves that fast and slow patterns see different ADHD signatures, and fusing them is the only way to catch them all.
